The premise is the problem: more agents don't always give better results. So "five or ten?" is the wrong question.

Here is why it's tempting and why it's wrong. Say a student asks, "Is the laser cutter free Thursday at 2, and what material settings do I use?" A split design might have a manual agent, a calendar agent, a booking agent and a coordinator. Every agent is its own model loop, and each one re-reads context and passes text to the others. That adds cost, and every hand-off is a chance to lose a detail.

Anthropic measured this on its multi-agent research system. Agents use about 4× the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent systems about 15× ([Anthropic](https://www.anthropic.com/news/multi-agent-research-system)). It also says multi-agent designs only pay off when the task is valuable enough to cover that cost. They fit breadth-first work that splits into independent directions. They fit poorly when agents need the same shared context or depend heavily on each other. Anthropic also warns that teams sometimes build elaborate multi-agent systems when better prompting of a single agent would have done as well ([Claude resources](https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them)).

Your assistant looks like the poor fit. The tasks are small, the steps depend on each other (check the calendar, then book), and your budget is tight. A sensible starting point is one agent with three tools (search the manuals, check the calendar, book). Add a second agent only if you can name a concrete problem a split would fix, such as manual text crowding out the booking context.

For your design review, ask "what specific failure does each extra agent fix, and what does it cost per request?" That is a stronger argument than any count.

Quick check: which part of your assistant's job could be a fixed workflow rather than an agent?

I can turn this into a lesson on workflows versus agents versus multi-agent systems if you'd like.

Sources:
- [Anthropic: multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/news/multi-agent-research-system)
- [Claude: Building multi-agent systems](https://claude.com/resources/articles/building-multi-agent-systems-when-and-how-to-use-them)
